title: How layer caching speeds up a build
summary: What stays cached and what is rebuilt after a code change.

steps.n: The developer changes one source file and builds the image again.
The first instructions are identical to the last build, so their layers come straight from the cache.
The dependency list did not change, so the cache is valid and the install step is skipped.
The changed file makes this layer different, so it and every following layer are rebuilt.
In a pipeline the cache is exported to a registry, so a clean runner can import it and avoid starting from zero.
Only the last layers were rebuilt, and the build took seconds instead of minutes.

title: Passing a secret to a build safely
summary: Why a secret mount leaves nothing in the image.

steps.n: The developer passes the file to the build as a secret, instead of as an ARG or COPY.
BuildKit mounts the secret in memory at /root/.npmrc, only while that RUN instruction executes.
The package manager reads the token from the mounted file and downloads private packages.
When the instruction ends the mount is removed, and nothing is written into the layer.
The image layers contain the installed packages but not the credentials.
docker history on the finished image shows no token, which a security scan can verify.

title: What happens when a container hits its memory limit
summary: From growth to restart.

steps.n: A cache without a size limit holds more entries every minute.
The cgroup limit is 512 MB, and the kernel starts to reclaim pages from the container, which slows it.
The application asks for pages that the kernel cannot give without going over the limit.
The kernel kills the largest process in the container with SIGKILL. The process has no chance to log or clean up.
Docker sees the exit, records exit code 137 and OOMKilled true in the container state.
If a policy is set, Docker restarts the container, and the cycle repeats until the cause is fixed.

title: A multi-architecture image
summary: How one tag works on amd64 and arm64.

steps.n: The developer asks for two platforms in a single build.
buildx builds one image per platform, with native builders or emulation, and the Go or Node tools target the right CPU.
The registry stores both images and a manifest list that maps platform to image digest.
A host asks for shop:1.4.2 and tells the registry its CPU architecture.
The registry returns the image that matches the host, so an arm64 laptop and an amd64 server use the same tag.
The binary matches the CPU, so the container starts. A single-platform image would fail with exec format error.

title: A gradual release with a feature flag
summary: Deploy first, release later, and switch off in seconds.

steps.n: The new code reaches production, but the flag is off, so nobody sees the new behaviour.
On each request the application asks the flag service whether the feature is on for this user, with a safe default.
The flag is first enabled for employees, who test the feature on the real system.
The flag is raised to one percent, chosen by a stable hash of the user id, while error rates are watched.
Error rate rises for the group with the flag on. The owner turns the flag off.
No redeploy is needed. The old behaviour returns for everyone, and the fix is released later.

title: Splitting tests across parallel jobs
summary: How a long test stage becomes short.

steps.n: The pipeline loads the durations recorded from earlier runs to know which tests are slow.
The first job gets a share of tests with a similar total duration.
The second job runs at the same time with the rest of the tests.
Each shard reports its results as soon as it finishes. Failure in any shard fails the stage.
Every shard writes new durations, so the next split is better balanced.
The pipeline combines the reports into one view. The stage takes the time of the slowest shard, not the sum.

title: A dependency cache keyed on the lockfile
summary: Why the key decides if the cache is safe.

steps.n: The pipeline computes a hash of package-lock.json. The hash is the cache key.
The cache store is asked for an entry with that exact key.
If the dependencies did not change, the saved downloads are restored in seconds.
If the lockfile changed, the key is new, so packages are downloaded and installed.
After a successful install the download directory is stored with the new key for later runs.
A branch-name key could serve old packages after a lockfile change. A lockfile hash cannot.

title: The Argo CD sync loop
summary: How the cluster is pulled towards the declared state.

steps.n: The developer changes the image tag in a manifest and merges it after review.
Argo CD polls the repository, or receives a notice, and sees a new revision of the desired state.
It reads the objects that currently run in the cluster.
Desired and live state are compared. The application is shown as OutOfSync with the exact differences.
With automated sync, Argo CD applies the new manifests, and Kubernetes rolls out the new version.
Argo CD watches the rollout and shows Synced and Healthy. If someone edits the cluster by hand, it shows the drift and can revert it.

title: Startup, readiness and liveness probes
summary: Which probe controls what.

steps.n: While the app is starting, the kubelet runs only the startup probe. Other probes wait until it succeeds.
After the application is up, the startup probe passes and the other probes begin.
The kubelet checks whether the app can serve traffic right now, for example by calling /ready.
If readiness fails, the Pod is taken out of the Service endpoints. It is not restarted.
A separate check detects a stuck process, for example a frozen event loop.
After several failures the kubelet restarts the container. A liveness check on the database would restart every Pod during a database fault.

title: A request inside a service mesh
summary: How sidecars add identity and encryption.

steps.n: The application calls http://payments as usual. It knows nothing about certificates.
The sidecar proxy catches the outgoing call and finds the destination from the mesh configuration.
Both proxies present short-lived certificates that name their workload identities and set up an encrypted connection.
The receiving proxy checks that the checkout identity is allowed to call POST /charge.
If the policy allows it, the proxy delivers the request to the payments container on the same Pod.
The reply goes back the same way, and both proxies record request counts, errors and latency for the mesh dashboards.

title: How the API server decides on a request
summary: Authentication, authorization and admission.

steps.n: The request reaches the API server with a client certificate or token.
The server works out who is calling: a user, a group or a service account.
RBAC looks for a role binding that grants the verb delete on pods in this namespace to the caller.
With no matching rule the answer is Forbidden. Kubernetes is deny by default, so nothing is allowed unless a rule says so.
Mutating and validating policies can change or reject the request, for example a rule against privileged Pods.
If every step passes, the change is stored in etcd and the caller receives the result.

title: From a claim to a mounted volume
summary: How storage reaches a Pod.

steps.n: The developer asks for 20 GB of storage with a storage class, without choosing a disk.
The storage class names a provisioner, which notices that a new claim needs a volume.
The provisioner creates the disk in the cloud or storage system and registers a PersistentVolume for it.
Kubernetes binds the claim to the new volume. The claim status changes from Pending to Bound.
The Pod refers to the claim by name and the scheduler places it on a node that can reach the disk.
The kubelet attaches and mounts the disk, and the container reads and writes data that survives restarts.

title: Testing layers for Terraform changes
summary: From a quick format check to a real deployment.

steps.n: The developer opens a pull request that changes a module.
Within seconds these tools find style problems, wrong references and invalid values, without any cloud call.
A scanner reads the code for public storage, open ports and missing encryption.
The plan is converted to JSON and policies reject, for example, public ingress to a database.
For widely used modules, terraform test creates real resources with random names in a separate account.
The test removes its resources, and the result is posted to the pull request before anyone reviews the change.

title: Renaming a resource without destroying it
summary: How a moved block keeps the object.

steps.n: The developer changes aws_db_instance.main to aws_db_instance.database for a naming rule.
Terraform does not find aws_db_instance.database in the state, so it sees a new resource.
The plan shows the old database destroyed and a new empty one created. This is the dangerous result.
The developer adds a block that says from the old address to the new address.
Terraform renames the entry in the state and the plan says no changes for the database.
The cloud resource stays untouched. Only the address in the state changed.

title: Reviewing and applying the same plan
summary: Why the pipeline applies the saved plan file.

steps.n: The author pushes the change and the pipeline starts.
The plan is saved to a file and its readable form is posted as a comment.
The reviewer checks the plan for destroys, replacements and surprises, not only the code.
After approval, the change is merged to the main branch.
The pipeline applies the saved plan, so exactly what was approved is what runs, even if the cloud changed meanwhile.
A final plan should say no changes. If it does not, the author looks at drift before the next change.

title: Splitting state to shorten plans
summary: Why separate stacks are faster and safer.

steps.n: The engineer needs an urgent change in the network.
Only the resources of the network stack are refreshed, so the plan takes about a minute.

steps.l: App deploy runs at the same time
steps.n: Another team applies the app stack at the same time, with its own state and lock, so no one waits.
The network stack exposes subnet ids as outputs, or they are found by tags with data sources.
The app stack reads what it needs, without owning or changing those resources.
A mistake in the app code cannot destroy the data stack, because it is a separate state with separate permissions.

title: Failover with a pilot light
summary: How a small standby grows when the main region fails.

steps.n: All users reach the primary region while data is replicated to the secondary region.
The secondary holds replicated data and minimal core services, so the cost stays low.
A regional outage makes the primary unreachable for users.
The DNS health check sees repeated failures and marks the primary unhealthy.
Automation, defined as code, builds out the application tier in the secondary region and promotes the replica database.
DNS now answers with the secondary region, and the recovery time is the time to scale up plus DNS caching.

title: A guardrail in a multi-account setup
summary: Why even an administrator cannot turn off audit logs.

steps.n: An administrator in a workload account tries to disable the audit trail.
The request is checked against permissions in the account and against policies attached higher up in the organisation.
A service control policy denies the stop and delete actions on audit logging for all accounts below it.
The administrator receives an error, whatever permissions they hold in the account.
Audit events continue to a central log archive that workload administrators cannot change.
The attempt itself is recorded and a detection rule notifies the security team.

title: A private bucket behind a CDN
summary: How a static site is served without making storage public.

steps.n: The browser connects to the CDN over HTTPS using the site domain and a valid certificate.
If the file is cached at this location, the CDN answers at once with no request to the origin.
On a miss, the CDN signs the origin request with its own identity.
The bucket policy allows reads only from this CDN distribution, and public access is blocked.
The object travels back to the edge with cache headers such as max-age.
The CDN returns the file and keeps a copy. Direct requests to the bucket address still fail.

title: How the cloud decides to allow a request
summary: Identity policy, resource policy and explicit deny.

steps.n: A role calls the storage API with temporary credentials.
The engine collects the identity policies, resource policy, permissions boundary and organisation policies.
Any matching deny ends the evaluation with a refusal, whatever allows exist.
If there is no deny, at least one statement must allow the action on this resource for this caller.
No matching allow means a default deny. The result is returned to the API.
On allow the object is read. On deny the error names the action and resource, and the audit log records the caller.

title: From a RED alert to a cause
summary: Using the standard dashboard to narrow down.

steps.n: The p99 for checkout is above its objective, and the alert links to the service dashboard.
Rate and errors look normal, but the duration panel shows a long tail, so the problem is slowness.
Filtering by version shows that only the new release is slow.
An example slow trace shows nine seconds waiting for a database connection.

steps.l: Jump to logs by trace id
steps.n: The trace id leads to a log line: connection pool exhausted, waiting for a free connection.
The on-call engineer rolls back or raises the pool size, and watches the same p99 panel recover.

title: How one label creates millions of series
summary: Why request ids do not belong on metrics.

steps.n: A developer adds the request id as a label on a request counter to help debugging.
Every request creates a label value never seen before, so the server must create a new time series each time.
The head block holds all active series in memory, and memory use rises with every request.
Dashboards that touch the metric time out, and the server restarts when it runs out of memory.
The operator lists metrics by series count and sees the counter with millions of series.
The label is removed, relabel rules drop the existing series, and the request id stays in logs and traces.

title: Tail sampling in a collector
summary: Keeping the traces that matter.

steps.n: Service A calls B and passes the trace context, so both record spans for the same trace.
Both services send their spans to a collector without deciding what to keep.
The collector holds spans in memory for a decision period, such as ten seconds, until the trace is complete.
If the trace has an error or took over a second, it is kept. Other traces are kept at a rate of five percent.
Only the chosen traces are written, so storage cost drops, but every failure is still available.
Dropped traces still count in metrics, so rates and error ratios remain correct.

title: The path of telemetry through a collector
summary: Receive, process, export.

steps.n: The application sends metrics, logs and traces with the OpenTelemetry protocol to the local collector.
The receiver turns the data into an internal format and passes it down the pipeline.
A processor adds the environment and cluster name, and removes fields that contain personal data.
Batches reduce the number of requests, and a memory limiter protects the collector under load.
Exporters send traces to the tracing system, metrics to the metrics store and logs to the log store.
Switching vendors only changes the exporter configuration. The application code stays the same.

title: A production readiness review
summary: How a team finds gaps before launch.

steps.n: The team asks for a review six weeks before launch, while design changes are still cheap.
Reviewers go through ownership, SLOs, alerts, capacity, rollout, recovery and security.
Questions are scenarios, such as what happens when the main dependency becomes slow, not yes or no checks.
Each gap becomes an item with an owner and a priority: must fix, should fix or accepted risk.
The team adds a rollback test, a runbook and an alert on user impact before the date.
Reviewers confirm the launch criteria are met, and the accepted risks are written down with a name.

title: Communication during an incident
summary: Who tells whom what and when.

steps.n: The commander opens an incident channel, names the roles and sets a severity based on impact.
Within minutes the comms lead posts a short update: who is affected, what we are doing, when the next update comes.
Responders work in their channel, make one change at a time and announce each change.
The operations lead tells the commander what was found. The commander decides about a rollback or a fail-over.
Updates follow the schedule even when there is no news, so support and customers are not left guessing.
After user metrics are verified, the all-clear goes out, and a blameless review is scheduled within a few days.

title: Load shedding under overload
summary: Protecting the service by refusing some work.

steps.n: A marketing email sends twice the normal traffic in a few minutes.
Requests wait for threads, latency grows, and clients retry, which adds even more load.
The service sees that its queue is longer than a limit, or that waiting time is above its target.
Optional requests get a quick 503 with a retry-after header, while checkout requests are still served.
Fewer calls reach the database, so it does not fall over and slow everything even more.
Well-behaved clients wait with exponential backoff and jitter, and the surge passes without a full outage.

title: Turning toil into automation
summary: How a repeated manual task is removed.

steps.n: The engineer clears a full disk by hand for the fourth time this month, following the same five steps.
The team records minutes per week spent on it. It is manual, repetitive and grows with the service.
A script with checks and a dry run runs the cleanup, and a review makes sure it is safe.
The disk-full alert starts the automation, which frees space and records what it did.
The on-call person receives a note instead of a page when the automation succeeds.
The team removes the source of the growth, so the automation becomes a safety net and not a daily habit.

title: Envelope encryption with a KMS
summary: How data is protected without exposing the master key.

steps.n: The application asks the key management service for a new data key under a named master key.
The service returns the data key in plain form and the same key encrypted under the master key.
The application encrypts the data locally with the plain key and then removes it from memory.
The encrypted data and the encrypted data key are stored together.
To read the data, the application sends the wrapped key to the KMS, which checks policy and logs the call.
Only roles allowed to use the master key can get the data key back, and the master key never leaves the service.

title: From a log event to a detection
summary: How a suspicious action becomes an alert.

steps.n: Every control plane call is sent within minutes to a central, protected log store.
A rule looks for audit logging being stopped, a new access key for a service user, or a root login.
The alert includes who, from which address, what changed and links to recent activity of that identity.
The analyst compares with the normal pattern and decides: true positive, false positive or unknown.
If it is real, the analyst disables the key or isolates the host reversibly, and keeps evidence.
Known automation is added to an allow list and the rule precision is tracked, so alerts stay trustworthy.

title: A secret scanner in the pipeline
summary: How a leaked token is stopped before it is merged.

steps.n: The developer accidentally includes an access key in a configuration file.
The scanner looks for known token formats and high-entropy strings in the changed lines.
The scanner reports the file and line, and the pipeline fails before the merge.
The message says what was found, and explains that the key must be treated as exposed, even if the change is never merged.
The developer revokes the key and gets a new one from the secret manager, which is read at run time.
The security team makes the scanner a required check and reviews how many findings occur each month.

title: An admission policy rejecting a Pod
summary: How a security rule is enforced before a workload runs.

steps.n: The developer applies a manifest whose container runs as root with a privileged flag.
The request passes authentication and RBAC, because the developer may create Deployments.
The API server sends the object to the policy engine for validation.
The engine finds that the rule requires non-root and no privileged mode, and the Pod breaks both.
The request is rejected with a clear message naming the rule and the field to change.
The developer sets runAsNonRoot and removes privileged. The Pod is accepted and scheduled.

title: What happens when you run a playbook
summary: From the command to a changed server, step by step.

steps.n: The engineer runs the command with an inventory and a playbook file.
The control node builds the host list and the ordered list of tasks for each host.
Ansible opens an SSH session to each managed node using the configured user and key.
For each task, a small Python module is copied to the managed node and run.
The module checks the current state and changes the system only if it differs from the request.
The module returns ok, changed or failed as JSON and is removed from the node.
The engineer sees counts per host, and a second run should show changed=0.

title: A template change triggering a reload
summary: How a handler runs once when configuration changes.

steps.n: The play reaches the task that renders the web server configuration.
The rendered text is compared with the file on the server and written only if it differs.
Because the file changed, the task queues the handler named Reload nginx.
Other tasks run. More tasks that change things can notify the same handler.
When all tasks finish for the host, the queued handlers are due.
The handler reloads the web server a single time, even if several tasks notified it.

title: How Vault protects a password in a run
summary: Where the secret is encrypted and where it appears in clear text.

steps.n: The password sits in the repository inside an encrypted vault file.
At run time the vault password is typed or fetched from a secret store, never read from the repository.
The control node reads the encrypted file and decrypts it in memory.
The task uses the value, and no_log keeps it out of console output and logs.
The password goes into a file on the host with strict owner and permissions.
The application reads the password locally. No other user on the host can read it.

title: A rolling update with a canary
summary: How serial batches and health checks limit damage.

steps.n: The play asks the load balancer to stop sending traffic to the canary host.
The new package is installed and the service restarted on that host only.
The play retries the health endpoint until it answers or the retry limit is reached.
If healthy, the canary goes back into the load balancer and receives real traffic.
The play repeats the same steps for the next batch, then the next.
If failures pass max_fail_percentage the play stops and the remaining hosts stay on the old version.

title: Terraform and Ansible working together
summary: Provisioning first, configuration second.

steps.n: Terraform asks the cloud to create networks, instances and security rules.
The cloud reports the new instance addresses, which Terraform records in state and outputs.
A dynamic inventory plugin lists current instances by tag or reads the outputs.
Ansible reads the inventory and groups the new hosts by role.
Ansible installs packages, writes files and starts services on each instance.
A clean second run shows changed=0. Later infrastructure changes go back through Terraform.

title: How a query reaches the data
summary: What the database does between your SQL and the answer.

steps.n: The client sends a query over a connection to the database.
The planner checks the syntax and estimates the cost of different ways to run it.
If an index fits and the query returns few rows, the plan uses it instead of scanning the table.
Needed pages come from memory if cached, or from disk if not.
The matching rows travel back to the client.
For an update the change is written to the log and flushed before the commit is acknowledged.

title: How a long transaction blocks a migration
summary: One idle session can stop a busy table.

steps.n: A reporting session starts a transaction and reads the orders table, then stays open.
A migration runs ALTER TABLE and needs a lock that conflicts with the open transaction.
The ALTER cannot proceed and waits for the report to finish.
Normal application queries now wait behind the queued ALTER.
The connection pool fills with waiting statements and the application times out.
Cancelling the migration releases the queue at once. Setting lock_timeout would have done this automatically.

title: Point-in-time recovery
summary: Restoring to the minute before a mistake.

steps.n: As changes are made, the write-ahead log segments are copied to the archive.
A full physical backup is taken regularly and stored with the archive.
After a bad delete at 14:00, the operator picks 13:59 as the recovery target.
The restore host receives the latest base backup taken before that time.
Archived log segments are applied until the target time is reached.
The operator checks the data, then promotes the restored server or copies back the missing rows.
